title: Five causes of action (18.13–18.18)
hook: every action you take has five causes, and you're only one of them
tomorrow: Three kinds of knowledge, action, doer (18.19–18.28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: renunciation vs relinquishment. Keep acting, let go of the outcome. Your line was let go of the fruit, not the act. Did you do one duty without gripping the result? Day two hundred twenty.
screen: `LET GO OF THE FRUIT, NOT THE ACT.`

segments.voice: Think of the best thing you ever did. The exam you aced, the meal you nailed, the moment you said exactly the right thing to a friend. Now ask: was that all you? You had a body that worked that day. Eyes and hands. Years of practice. And maybe something you can't name: the right question on the paper, the ripe tomatoes at the market, the friend being ready to hear it. Chapter eighteen takes any action at all and counts its causes. It finds five. And you are only one.
screen: `THE BEST THING YOU EVER DID.` → `WAS IT ALL YOU?` → `THE GITA COUNTS FIVE CAUSES.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen: learn from me the five causes for the completion of every action, as taught in the Samkhya teaching. Verse fourteen lists them. First, adhishthana, the seat: the body, the base where the action happens. Second, karta, the doer: the one who says I'm doing this. Third, the various instruments: the senses and the mind. Fourth, the many different efforts: the movements, the breaths, the energies that actually carry the action out. And fifth, daiva. Daiva is hard to translate. It can mean the divine, providence, or what some call fate or luck: the part that's beyond your control. Different teachers read it differently, some as God's hand, some as the weight of past karma. Verse fifteen: whatever action a person begins with body, speech or mind, right or wrong, these five are its causes. And verse sixteen is the turn. So the one who sees themselves as the only doer, because their understanding is untrained, doesn't see. That's the lesson in one line. You're one cause among five. This cuts two ways. When things go well, it takes the air out of pride: you had help, from your body, your senses, your effort, and something beyond all of them. And when things go badly, it takes some weight off guilt: not everything was yours to control. Verse eighteen adds a small map: knowing, the known and the knower set action in motion, and the instrument, the act and the doer hold it together. Tomorrow we'll sort those by the three threads. That's the word today: five causes of action.
screen: `FIVE CAUSES FOR EVERY ACTION.` · `SEAT, DOER, INSTRUMENTS, EFFORT.` · `THE FIFTH: DAIVA, BEYOND YOU.` · `WHO SEES ONLY 'I' DOESN'T SEE.` · then, large: `FIVE CAUSES OF ACTION.`

segments.voice: Sit, and take one breath as an action. Notice the five. The seat: your body, sitting. The doer: the sense that I am breathing. The instruments: the nose, the lungs, the attention. The effort: the muscles moving, the air flowing. And the fifth: the part you didn't make and can't explain, that there is air, that you're alive to breathe it. Let the breath keep going on its own. The bell holds the time.
Five causes of action. Gita eighteen, fourteen: the seat, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and daiva, the unseen fifth. The doer is only one of five.
Your line: not I alone. Today, when something goes well, name one other cause. When something goes wrong, name one too. Day two hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers use Gita 18.13–18.16 to loosen the sense of being the sole doer, so that success doesn't feed pride and failure doesn't crush; many devotees offer the results of their actions to God for the same reason.

myth: the Gita says the doer is the only real cause of an action
the doer is one of five; verse 16 says seeing only yourself is not seeing.
daiva can be read as the divine, providence, or fate
teachers read it differently, some as God's hand, some as past karma.

verse 15: right or wrong, these five are its causes.

fork.setup: you've just done something brilliant, and everyone's congratulating you. what would Gita 18.16 say?
options: take all the credit: you did it.
you're one cause among five; the one who sees only 'I' doesn't see.
it was only luck, so you did nothing.
fork.reveal: one cause among five. the Gita doesn't erase the doer; it just refuses to make the doer the whole story.

original.note: Sanskrit: daiva, of the gods, the divine, providence or fate; the fifth cause of action in Gita 18.14.

trapdoor: what you thought: I do my actions, full stop.
what it means: every action has five causes, and the doer is only one of them.
what a scholar hears: 18.14 names adhishthana, karta, karana, cheshta and daiva, attributed to Samkhya; commentators differ on daiva, from the divine or the inner controller to accumulated karma.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.15–18.16 (the one who sees only themselves as doer does not see)
Bhagavad Gita 18.18 (knowledge, known, knower; instrument, act, agent)

notes: 18.17 (the one free of ego-sense, even if he kills these people, does not kill and is not bound) is deliberately left out: it is easily misread out of context and deserves a Keeper's framing if it is added.
